question: to the Commission Şerban Dimitrie Sturdza (ECR) Subject:

The Commission proposed the digital omnibus with the aim of simplifying some obligations under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on artificial intelligence and thus reducing the administrative burden on European businesses and strengthening competitiveness. Generative AI systems are accessible to minors and can create or recommend text, images, audio and videos. These systems pose risks to children, including exposure to unsuitable content, behavioural manipulation, the creation of harmful content and effects on mental development. The protection of children in the digital environment is guaranteed by Articles 24 and 14(3) of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, which enshrine the right of the child to protection and the right of parents to ensure that children are educated according to their convictions. 1.

How will the Commission ensure that the simplification of the AI Act through the digital omnibus does not lower the level of protection of minors from generative artificial intelligence systems, in particular with regard to exposure to age-inappropriate content?
What concrete support is the Commission offering to allow parents to effectively exercise their right to control and consent to the exposure of their young children to these types of systems?

How will consistency be ensured between the simplification measures and the obligations already provided for in the Digital Services Act with regard to the protection of minors, so that no regulatory gaps emerge?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The AI Act1 protects children by introducing safeguards for the development and use of AI systems. It prohibits AI systems that manipulate, deceive or exploit children’s vulnerabilities with the objective or the effect of materially distorting children’s behaviour in a manner likely to lead to significant harm2. AI systems used in education are high-risk and must comply with requirements on, among others, risk management, transparency and human oversight. The AI Omnibus does not undermine the high level of protection that the AI Act provides. It strengthens children’s protection by prohibiting AI systems that generate child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate content3. The Digital Services Act (DSA)4 sets harmonised rules for a safe, predictable and trusted online environment, including for children, and is unaffected by the AI Omnibus. Article 28 DSA requires providers of online platforms accessible to minors to put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors, on their service. The Commission Guidelines on the protection of minors5 set out measures that, in the Commission’s view, providers should implement to comply with that obligation. The AI Act and DSA are complementary and together ensure a high level of child protection in the EU6. The Commission also fosters media literacy and digital learning through the European strategy for a Better Internet for Kids7 (BIK+), the Safer Internet Centres and the BIK platform8. These support children and young people in, among others, building critical digital skills and using social media and AI responsibly. They also equip parents, caregivers, teachers and educators with the knowledge and tools to support children online.
